Where it began

Glenn Phillips was born on 6 December 1996 in the South African city of East London, and moved to New Zealand with his family when he was five. He played his school cricket at Sacred Heart College in Auckland before going to the 2016 Under-19 World Cup.

He made an early splash for Auckland. In his first Super Smash season, 2016–17, he scored more runs than anyone, 369 of them, and an unbeaten 116 against Central Districts made him only the second player after Hamish Marshall to score hundreds in all three formats of New Zealand's domestic game, and the first to manage it inside a single season.

The player

He batted right-handed, bowled off-spin and could take the gloves when needed. His Test debut came out of the blue at Sydney in January 2020, when he was flown in as cover and found himself playing; he top-scored in the first innings with 52. His second Test did not arrive until the tour of Bangladesh late in 2023, but he made the wait worthwhile, taking his first Test wickets, four of them in an innings, and scoring 87 and 40 not out in the next match.

On 18 June 2026 he reached his first Test hundred against England at The Oval, and finished on exactly 100. By November 2026 he had played 19 Tests, with 956 runs at 35.41, a hundred and five fifties, and 33 wickets at 31.03 with a best of 5 for 45. He had also held 20 catches.

What made him special

In the short game he could take an attack apart. His 46-ball hundred against the West Indies in 2020 was the fastest by a New Zealander in a T20 international, and he matched that pace against India in October 2026 on his way to 107, finishing that series with 341 runs, a record for a two-team T20 series. He helped New Zealand to the final of the 2021 T20 World Cup and to the semi-final of the 2023 World Cup.

For a while the bowling was very much the second string. When he joined Otago in 2022 he said plainly that he wanted to become a proper all-rounder. Thirty-three Test wickets later, it is fair to say he meant it.

Away from the middle

He played franchise cricket all over the world, from the Caribbean Premier League and The Hundred to Major League Cricket and the IPL. At Otago he played alongside his younger brother, Dale.

And finally

He batted, he bowled, he kept wicket, and in September 2025 he earned a pilot's licence as well. His captains could be forgiven for wondering whether there was any job, on the field or above it, he could not turn his hand to.
